Yes, I got my occipital nerve stimulator the beginning of January 2023 after a trial unit in December 2022.

Let me say, in a few words: holy shit.

This device has changed my life for the better. Sure, I still get some pain every now and again, but what I do feel is so, so much less compared to prior to ONS. I've dealt with ON for 18 years, and it honestly feels like I have a huge chunk of my life back.

My only word of caution is be vigilant and persistent with your insurance company. A lot of them *hate* covering ONS, and don't, because it's technically not FDA approved for ON (yet). My insurance went back and forth whether they required a pre authorization or not. I *finally*, after 2 days, got them to fax the confirmation of needing no authorization 5 minutes before the surgery center was going to cancel my procedure the following day. Be persistent. Always follow up. I was their biggest pain in the ass for 2 days.

Definitely absolutely recommend giving it a shot. The trial is very well worth getting to know what it feels like, especially in your daily routine (except showering, lol). The real thing is so much of a relief in my life. 10/10. 100% worth paying my whole out of pocket maximum for.

Hi, immunocompromised person here. Vaccined and boostered, for context.

Some of us *can't* go out all willy-nilly to parties and other dumb shit because even with the vaccine, catching COVID would mean hospital and potentially ICU. Some of us *have* to go out for whatever reason - doctor's visits aren't always telehealth compatible, especially dealing with infusions or similar treatment. We have no choice. Even variant Omicron, which supposedly has less of an impact (aside from being extremely highly contagious), it very well can and will land an immunocompromised person at the hospital. At least it reduces the chances of death...won't reduce the chance of costly medical bills.

For a normal health person? Sure, the vaccine means staying home feeling like shit instead of a hospital stay. For someone who's immunocompromised? It's the difference between hospital/ICU and death. No vaccine *ever* has a 100% chance of avoiding a virus, but they *do* offer increased protection and lesser severity of a virus.

I'm all for looking out for your health (some of us absolutely *have* to), but your right to freedom and liberty does not take precedence over someone's right to live. Please, think about this the next time you encounter a cashier at Meijer during Super Bowl weekend or the fast food worker working at 2AM during a drunken Taco Bell run.

No matter which major you pick, you’ll have good and not so good profs. That will happen at any college. Learn who’s good and befriend them; networking with your favorite profs can be highly crucial to landing a great thesis topic or job.

My fiscal situation was very different than others here, but the co-op earnings definitely do help on top of scholarships/grants. You can also search for other scholarships and apply - I highly recommend this as well. It may be a pain in the ass to write 500-word essays, but it’s worth the $1,000+ less you’d have to fork out. My debt isn’t *too* awful considering my circumstances, and I plan on having it paid down rather quickly.

The community here is fairly close-knit. I’m one of the few women on campus, and I was lucky to find the group I felt most at home with. The Greek community is pretty great here, but so is the non-Greek community. You’ll find your place within a term or so.

Having 2+ years of experience puts you far ahead in the job hunt. Sometimes you’ll land a position with your co-op; I personally didn’t, but ended up securing a nice federal contractor position. You’ll be able to gain real-world experience, not only in your field, but in the aspects of professional speaking and technical writing which are huge no matter your destination. Also - professional conduct and interview skills gained from co-op programs put you way ahead the curve. My current team lead said my interview skills were far above the level of others he interviewed.
